Ch . 7
One can imagine varying levels of skepticism by courts evaluating 
agency factfinding. On the one hand, one might make a case for great 
deference to agency factual determinations. Most challenges to agency 
action are conducted in an appellate-style of review, a venue not designed 
for thorough-going second-guessing of factual determinations. 
Furthermore, if agencies are created in order to harness a particular kind 
of expertise, deferring to factual determinations seems to follow from that 
objective. On the other hand, if courts are to protect against arbitrary or 
lawless behavior by agencies, factual determinations cannot be presumed 
correct without judicial assessment. In practice, cases concerning the 
appropriate standard of review for agency factfinding often depend on 
understanding the structure of section 706 of the APA or a statute-specific 
scope-of-review provision.
a. The Substantial Evidence Test
Section 706(2)(E) authorizes reviewing courts in formal proceedings to 
hold unlawful and set aside agency action, findings, and conclusions found 
to be * * * unsupported by substantial evidence [.]” In addition, section 706 
generally requires that such a determination shall be made on “the whole 
record or those parts of it cited by a party.” 5 U.S.C. § 706. Agency-specific 
statutes also sometimes specify that a court shall apply the substantial 
evidence test.
The leading precedent on the APA’s substantial evidence provision 
arises out of the complex framework of labor statutes enacted by Congress 
in the pre-APA era. In the Wagner Act of 1935, Congress created the 
National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) and provided that “the findings of 
the Board as to facts, if supported by evidence, shall be conclusive.” The 
Supreme Court construed the Act to require NLRB determinations to be 
supported by “substantial evidence,” Washington, Virginia & Maryland 
Coach Co. V. NLRB, 301 U.S. 142, 147 (1937), and described “substantial 
evidence” to mean something “more than a mere scintilla * * * or such 
relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to 
support a conclusion,” Consolidated Edison Co. v. NLRB, 305 U.S. 197, 229 
(1938).
Critics claimed that these judicial glosses on the text of the Wagner 
Act were translated into reflexive deference in practice. They contended 
that courts approved Board determinations whenever they could find 
record evidence that, viewed in isolation, substantiated agency findings. 
These charges formed the backdrop against which Congress enacted the 
APA in 1946, as well as a second labor statute, the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947. 
They also formed the backdrop against which the Court considered the 
substantial evidence standard in the following classic case.
